entries.title: Pirates, Bandits and Raiders
entries.excerpt: Pirates and bandits exist on the margins of human space, surviving in the gaps left by failing infrastructure, fading oversight, and the slow decay of interstellar connectivity....
entries.search: Pirates and bandits exist on the margins of human space, surviving in the gaps left by failing infrastructure, fading oversight, and the slow decay of interstellar connectivity. Their structure ranges from single-ship operations with desperate crews to loosely organized factions flying under self-declared banners of independence, though most lack recognized territory and rarely hold captured colonies for long before they're dismantled by central authority. Their ships are as varied as their motives: repurposed industrial freighters, stolen civilian craft, gutted mining rigs retrofitted with weapon mounts, or even old military hulls held together by luck and stolen parts. Some strike out of desperation, others for profit, and a few under ideological pretenses: anti-government, separatist, or anarchist. Most, however, simply want to survive, and their targets reflect that. They prey on the weak and the isolated: drifting vessels in local space, colonies left out of rotation too long, outposts with minimal defenses and even springing traps on ships exiting from Gates lacking in proper security. Functioning gates are rarely targeted, not out of mercy, but because disrupting a gate disrupts their own routes just as badly. Stolen cargo is either used, sold on black markets, or held for ransom. Fuel, food, and munitions are scrounged from ambushes or traded in shadowy backrooms of fringe colonies that look the other way. To the average colonist, pirates are a terrifying unknown. To experienced ship crews, theyâ€™re more of a wildcard with some encounters ending in tense stand-offs and others in blood. Theyâ€™re not everywhere, but theyâ€™re common enough that no vessel travels without at least one mounted weapon and a crew ready to use it.

entries.title: Outposts
entries.excerpt: Outposts are small, often isolated installations that serve as utility points throughout human space. Unlike colonies, they are not intended for long-term habitation or large po...
entries.search: Outposts are small, often isolated installations that serve as utility points throughout human space. Unlike colonies, they are not intended for long-term habitation or large populations. Most are staffed by fewer than a dozen personnel at any given time, if at all. Some outposts operate unmanned, visited only when ships dock to refuel, repair, or drop off rotating maintenance crews. Their functions vary widely: some monitor junction systems with multiple corridor links, others serve as rest stops, emergency shelters, or orbital watchpoints for military or survey activity. A few are embedded into asteroids for resource sampling or data relay. Outposts are typically built by nearby colonies or by central government agencies and powered by solar panels and battery systems, with a small few being powered by reactors. Supplies are delivered intermittently by ship, making them dependent on external support. While rarely intentionally abandoned, many outposts fall off the official registry once their purpose fades or routes shift, leaving them vulnerable to decay or reappropriation by scavengers and pirates. Most threats they face are environmental; systemic failures, radiation exposure, or natural hazards, but remote locations sometimes attract hostile attention. Life at an outpost, for those who live there, is routine shift work: lonely, quiet, and largely thankless.

entries.title: Space Stations
entries.excerpt: Space stations serve as larger, more developed variants of outposts or smaller Civilian settlements. Unlike colonies, they typically do not sustain large civilian populations an...
entries.search: Space stations serve as larger, more developed variants of outposts or smaller Civilian settlements. Unlike colonies, they typically do not sustain large civilian populations and instead generally house at most 25-75 individuals, plus the transient presence of visiting ship crews. Those who live aboard stations may have varying roles: some work as mechanics at nearby Gates, others at might work at nearby military installations, research platforms, or regional relay points for logistics and communication. Usually only a small group of those living on a Space Station have jobs aboard the space station; most work off-station in nearby local space, returning only after the end of their shifts. Ownership is usually centralized, with the core government overseeing most stations, though some may be administered by local colonies depending on their region and purpose. Their locations are strategically chosen, to act as critical â€œfirst stopsâ€ for arriving vessels or be for easy access to multiple different locations nearby. Space stations are not self-sufficient. They rely heavily on external supply runs and consistent maintenance to remain operational, though with proper care they are built to endure for decades. Accessibility ranges from open ports to heavily restricted facilities depending on the stationâ€™s purpose. While life aboard a station is utilitarian and often monotonous, crews may include a mix of maintenance personnel, engineers, medical staff, shopkeepers, scientists, and security, reflecting the stationâ€™s specific needs.

entries.title: Ships
entries.excerpt: Interstellar ships form the backbone of humanityâ€™s crumbling infrastructure, ferrying people, supplies, and information between scattered Colonies via the unstable Corridors n...
entries.search: Interstellar ships form the backbone of humanityâ€™s crumbling infrastructure, ferrying people, supplies, and information between scattered Colonies via the unstable Corridors network. Their crews are often the only thread connecting humanityâ€™s fractured outposts. Ship Types Ships vary from small haulers and corvettes to large freighters and carrier-class transports, though all are built for function over form. â€¢ Civilian ships are modular, refitted constantly, and often patchwork relics of older designs. â€¢ Military, paramilitary, and corporate vessels also exist, though even these tend to be underpowered, overused, and stretched thin. Corridor Travel Fir safe travel, ships must enter and exit Corridors via Gates, which stabilize the journey and reduce the risk of catastrophic failure. While in transit, ships are exposed to Corridor Radiation, requiring robust hull shielding and post-travel decontamination procedures. Internal systems often suffer malfunctions during transit with crew intervention being mandatory for repairs, calibration, and maintaining life support. Crew Roles A typical crew is lean but skilled. Roles often include: â€¢ Navigator/Pilot â€“ Plots transit routes and handles gate alignments. â€¢ Mechanic/Engineer â€“ Maintains ship integrity, handles emergency repairs, and monitors life support. â€¢ Medical Officer â€“ Treats injuries and monitors radiation exposure. â€¢ Cargo/Systems Officer â€“ Manages supplies, ballast, and power distribution. â€¢ Captain/Commander â€“ Makes route decisions, enforces priorities, and often negotiates at each stop. Smaller ships may consolidate roles; larger ones may have redundancy or expanded teams. Life as a Ship Crew Life aboard ship is tense, exhausting, and dangerous. Crew members live in close quarters, share limited amenities, and face constant equipment degradation. Crews often operate under tight contracts from colonial governments, Earth authorities, or corporate sponsors but many run independent. Salvage, courier runs, emergency resupply, or medical retrievals are common assignments. Not all of them are above-board. Ship crews are respected and pitied in equal measure. Their work keeps the system functioning, but at significant personal cost. Many ship crews are superstitious, especially about routes that have gone â€œdarkâ€ before, gates with a history of failure, or ships that returned in ways they shouldn't have. Crews trade stories, warnings, and unofficial maps wherever they dock, information can often more valuable than money. Risk and Reward Every run carries the risk of Corridor collapse, radiation overexposure, piracy, or mechanical failure. But for many, a ship job is the only chance at movement, purpose, or upward mobility Veteran crews rarely retire. Most either vanish, get stuck somewhere after one too many failed jobs without a functioning ship or enough money to buy one; or become permanent fixtures in the darker corners of a colony bar, unable to escape their past.

entries.title: Gates
entries.excerpt: Gates are colossal human-made megastructures designed to stabilize and hold open Corridors for reliable interstellar travel. Without them, Corridor entry and exit is nearly impo...
entries.search: Gates are colossal human-made megastructures designed to stabilize and hold open Corridors for reliable interstellar travel. Without them, Corridor entry and exit is nearly impossible or catastrophically unsafe. Purpose and Function Gates create a stable entry or exit point into a Corridor by anchoring it in place and supplying vast amounts of power to maintain the connection. Gates also emit a radio frequency known as a "Gate Beacon", which by design can only travel relatively short distances and is broadcast directly into its connected Corridor. Ships are equipped with sensors for picking up and tracking Gate Beacons to aid in Corridor navigation. â€¢ Without a gate, Corridors remain unusable for most vessels. Entry leads to uncontrolled, often fatal results. â€¢ Gates are generally located near colonies, stations, or key sectors and are crucial for maintaining transport, communication, and supply lines. In some rare cases, Gates can be found in otherwise empty systems, existing for the sole purpose of linking two or more Corridor routes together to further connect the Corridor network. Construction and Limitations â€¢ Building a gate is a massive logistical effort requiring specialized equipment, a stable orbit or staging point, and long-term maintenance infrastructure. â€¢ Once constructed, gates cannot be moved under their own power. However, they can be relocated short distances with auxiliary tug fleets if a Corridor shifts within the same system. â€¢ If a Corridor shifts out of range, the gate becomes effectively useless unless it later returns nearby. â€¢ Gates may be repaired and reactivated if a Corridor shifts back into a reachable area, but alignment is never exact and always requires re-positioning. Failure and Risk Gates have several risks associated with them, from destabilization or failure of their attached Corridor to technical malfunction and breakdown. â€¢ If a gateâ€™s power fails or control systems destabilize, the Corridor may collapse or shift prematurely, posing catastrophic risk to ships in transit. â€¢ Older gates, especially those built during humanityâ€™s rapid expansion period, are more prone to malfunctions and radiation leakage into their local systems. â€¢ Gates at dead routes, where Corridors have collapsed or shifted irreversibly are often left to float abandoned, unusable but too expensive to dismantle. Decontamination and Medical Operational Gates include decontamination infrastructure for handling Corridor Radiation exposure and basic medical care aboard their Concourse: - Hull Cleaning system - Crew medical screening and quarantine - Basic medical treatment - Radiation scrubbing Only ships passing through a gated exit receive full decontamination. Those using natural or emergency exits risk spreading contamination or dying from exposure. More advanced medical ailments or injuries often require treatment or specialized care not available at Gates. Rest and Recreation The majority of gates have a (tiny in comparison to the rest of the Gate structure) facility attached to the main Gate "ring" with docking capabilities for Ships. These facilities, referred to as the 'Gate Concourse' is generally where the Gate Technicians live and work, though Gate Concourses often also include things like shops, restaurants, lounges, bars; with some more 'prominent' Gates even being home to things like Hotels or recreational areas such as movie theaters, arcades, and so on. Strategic Value â€¢ Gates are among the most valuable and contested infrastructure in human space. â€¢ Their control determines who lives, who starves, and who remains connected to the rest of humanity. â€¢ Many derelict or decaying colonies still maintain minimal personnel around gate structures, hoping for a Corridor to shift back into range.

entries.title: Corridors
entries.excerpt: Corridors are naturally occurring interstellar pathways that allow faster-than-light travel between distant regions of the galaxy. Humanity did not create them, only discovered ...
entries.search: Corridors are naturally occurring interstellar pathways that allow faster-than-light travel between distant regions of the galaxy. Humanity did not create them, only discovered and exploited them. Though the mechanics are not fully understood, ships entering a Corridor are able to traverse immense distances in a fraction of the time; usually days or weeks, compared to centuries by conventional means. While poorly understood, it is believed that Corridors are an effect of the universe itself and are therefore just as old and naturally occurring. Structure and Function â€¢ Corridors have two or more stable entry/exit regions (informally referred to as "positions" or "points"). â€¢ Travel through a Corridor is one of the only methods of practical interstellar transit. â€¢ Their interior is hostile, a void like medium saturated with Corridor Radiation, requiring hardened ships and constant maintenance. â€¢ Ships must exit through a gate; entry and exit without one is nearly suicidal, often resulting in catastrophic loss Gate Usage â€¢ Gates are massive human-built structures that anchor Corridors in place, forcing them open and stable for transit. â€¢ Without a gate, Corridors become inaccessible, unpredictable, or dangerous to enter. â€¢ Gates are resource-intensive, immobile, and require continual power and upkeep. â€¢ If a Corridor shifts or closes, a gate may become useless, requiring recovery and salvage or abandonment. Shifting and Collapse â€¢ Corridors naturally shift between a set of rough positions (usually 8â€“12). The shift is unpredictable, but known routes may return over time. â€¢ Even when a Corridor shifts back to a previous position, it never returns to the exact coordinates. Gates must be relocated within the system to match the new offset. â€¢ A collapse is different from a shift. When a Corridor collapses: Â Â Â Â â—¦ One of its former positions is permanently lost. Â Â Â Â â—¦ It either adds a new position to its rotation or becomes a new Corridor entirely, with different entry/exit points. Â Â Â Â â—¦ Collapsed Corridors no longer emit Corridor Radiation and cannot be reaccessed. Other Notes â€¢ Human expansion depended heavily on stable Corridors. As their reliability degraded, so did interstellar infrastructure. â€¢ Colonies stranded by shifting or collapsing Corridors often suffer total isolation, leading to slow decline or death. â€¢ Some Corridors still offer partial stability, allowing travel with heavy risk; but remain the only option for keeping distant colonies alive.

entries.title: Colonies
entries.excerpt: Human colonies are scattered across dozens of star systems, founded during the peak of interstellar expansion when Corridors were considered stable and Gates were plentiful. The...
entries.search: Human colonies are scattered across dozens of star systems, founded during the peak of interstellar expansion when Corridors were considered stable and Gates were plentiful. Their survival now depends heavily on whether their Corridor routes remain active. They generally sustain a population of anywhere between 50-250, but rarely more due to resource strain. Unfortunately; this means that almost no colony has the population size to sustainably reproduce on its own if left isolated. Structure and Environment Colonies are almost always enclosed, industrial, and highly functional-prioritizing longevity and utility over comfort. Most colonies are built into hardened structures on planetary surfaces, inside asteroids, or on other naturally occurring celestial bodies. Windows are rare, aesthetics rarer. Life is cramped and resource-regulated, with many Colonies relying on strict maintenance cycles, rationed supplies, and relentless work routines to stay viable. Atmospheric and gravity systems vary; some use planetary conditions, while others rely on different levels of artificial life support. Colonies are generally designed to extract raw materials, grow food, generate energy, and manage relay infrastructure essential to human survival; as well as supporting human populations across the galaxy Population and Culture Most colonies are populated by a mix of laborers, engineers, security forces, and administrators. Civilian life revolves around survival, utility work, and maintaining infrastructure. Entertainment and culture exist but are minimal and usually improvised. Some colonies are stilly explicitly loyal to Earth, while others have drifted into pragmatic isolation or outright de facto independence. Supply and Isolation Colonies require supplies, information, and personnel from other systems to remain sustainable over long term. If a Corridor shifts or collapses, a colony can be cut off indefinitely, losing all contact with the wider network. If the Corridor returns, it often does so too late. Many such colonies are found dead or nearly so. Reclaimed colonies are sometimes resettled or salvaged, with remnants of the previous population still present-sometimes alive, usually not. Quarantine and Hazards Disease, resource collapse, environmental breach, and structural decay are common risks among Colonies. Some enact quarantine procedures during incidents, though enforcement varies as does effectiveness. Rumors of "ghost colonies" persist; places that went dark and were later found abandoned, their interiors intact, but with no sign of where the inhabitants went, though no official evidence exists to support these.

entries.title: FTL and Intra System Travel
entries.excerpt: FTL and In-System Travel Corridors are the only means of faster-than-light (FTL) travel. They allow ships to move between star systems, but they never exit directly at a colony....
entries.search: FTL and In-System Travel Corridors are the only means of faster-than-light (FTL) travel. They allow ships to move between star systems, but they never exit directly at a colony. Corridors open wherever their current anchor position happens to be in the target system which is often far from inhabited locations. Once a ship exits the corridor, it must travel to its destination (colony, outpost, station) using sub-light engines. These can handle astronomical distances efficiently, but not instantly. Shorter intra-system travel (e.g. from a gate to a nearby orbital station) may take hours to a day. Longer treks across the system, say from the gate to a colony several AU away, can take several days to a week, depending on ship specs and fuel reserves. This sub-light travel is relatively safe. Aside from basic risks like equipment failure, fuel mismanagement, or navigation errors, most corridor-related threats like Corridor Radiation and Static Fog do not persist outside of the corridor itself. Once in normal space, crews only contend with standard spacefaring hazards. Unlike Corridor Radiation or Static Fog, Vacuum Bloom remains a wildcard in intra-system travel. Since it drifts and latches to heat and metal, it may be present in systems with recent ship traffic or poor decontamination enforcement, but itâ€™s not exclusive to corridor zones. It can spread in normal space if introduced by contaminated ships; including spreading to inhabited areas such as colonies, space stations or outposts. Outposts and stations are common waypoints between gates and settlements, especially in sprawling systems with distant colonies. These midpoints serve as additional: - Refueling stops - Emergency repair docks - Relay points for physical data or small-scale cargo - Rest locations Travel times and system layout matter. Even if a colony is â€œconnectedâ€ via corridor, actual arrival depends on local infrastructure, fuel, crew skill, and distance. There is no â€œdirect drop-off.â€

entries.title: Pervasive Threat: Corridor Radiation
entries.excerpt: Even when a Corridor is stable and a Gate is fully operational, the internal medium of the Corridor is an actively hostile environment. The following subsections detail the pers...
entries.search: Even when a Corridor is stable and a Gate is fully operational, the internal medium of the Corridor is an actively hostile environment. The following subsections detail the persistent, unavoidable environmental threats that all crews must be prepared to mitigate during every transit. These are not risks that can be avoided, only managed. Corridor Radiation is composed of exotic particulate matter that is invariably present in all active Corridors. It is an aggressive agent that degrades technology and biological tissue, making effective shielding and decontamination procedures absolutely essential for survival. Effects of Exposure â€¢ On Ship Systems: The radiation has a corrosive effect on exposed hull materials and causes significant electrical instability, particularly impacting sensitive navigation and power systems. Over time, it also degrades optical sensors. â€¢ On Human Biology: For unshielded personnel, exposure is agonizing and rapidly fatal. Initial symptoms, including intense surface burns and disorientation, appear within hours. This progresses to acute radiation syndrome, systemic organ failure, tissue necrosis, and ultimately death. The primary method for managing this threat is the use of robust ship shielding during transit and mandatory passage through the full decontamination facilities present at all gated exits. Ships forced to use ungated exit points face a significant risk of lethal contamination. Static Fog is a rare but severe electro-magnetic storm system that can form within Corridors or linger near their exit points. Its primary danger is the systematic and silent disabling of critical ship functions, creating a state of cascading failure. â€¢ Minor Encounters: A vessel passing through a mild Fog will experience disruption of sensors, communications, and navigation systems, requiring manual intervention from the crew. â€¢ Severe Encounters: A severe Fog can be catastrophic, powerful enough to fry a ship's core power systems, disable life support entirely, and even cause hull ruptures through extreme magnetic shearing forces. Unlike Corridor Radiation, Static Fog does not directly harm biological tissue. Instead, it creates a silent, system-wide failure state that is equally lethal, leaving a crew to face depressurization, power loss, and navigational blindness in an already hazardous environment. These internal hazards, both pervasive and sporadic, demonstrate that survival is not guaranteed even on a successful transit, leading to ancillary threats that can follow a vulnerable ship into normal space. The dangers of Corridor travel do not end upon exiting the transit medium. The network itself, by its very nature, creates vulnerabilities that foster both biological and human threats. These hazards can spread between systems via contaminated ships or prey upon the isolation and weakness of travelers in the vast distances between secure ports. Vacuum Bloom is a non-sentient, fungus-like organism that drifts through deep space as a nearly undetectable cloud of spores. It is an indifferent hazard, posing no intelligent threat, but its biological imperatives make it a dire risk to all human infrastructure. The organism passively seeks heat and metal, causing it to latch onto ships, stations, and colonies. â€¢ On Structures: Once attached, the Bloom spreads like a voracious rot, consuming infrastructure from within. If an infestation is not contained immediately, it can render an entire vessel or habitat a total loss. â€¢ On Humans: The inhalation of Vacuum Bloom spores is fatal. The organism grows within the lungs, causing rapid respiratory failure and toxic shock, after which it consumes the victim's body. The spread of Vacuum Bloom is a direct consequence of ship traffic moving between systems, an ever-present biological risk carried on the hulls of the unwary. The decay of interstellar infrastructure, fading governmental oversight, and the profound isolation of many colonies and trade routes create ideal conditions for piracy. These groups range from single desperate crews to loosely organized factions. Their vessels are a direct reflection of their opportunistic nature: a patchwork of repurposed industrial freighters, stolen civilian craft, and gutted mining rigs retrofitted with weapon mounts. Their methods and targets are dictated by pragmatism. They prey on the weak: isolated vessels, remote outposts with minimal defenses, and colonies struggling with severed supply lines. They rarely attack well-defended, operational Gates, as these structures are as vital to their own mobility as they are to legitimate commerce. Their existence is a constant, unpredictable human threat in the gaps of a failing system. From immediate predators to slower biological decay, these ancillary threats pave the way for the ultimate, systemic hazard created by the Corridor network: isolation.
